traveler: Leo Africanus (al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan al-Fasi al-Gharnati)
title: Two Countries and No Grave: from Granada to Timbuktu to the font of Saint Peter's
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Granada, a birth after the surrender
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; Wikipedia gives c. 1494 and World History Encyclopedia c. 1485, the year back-calculated from his self-reported ages at later events and never from a birth record
stops.campa: A son is born to the family al-Wazzan in Granada, and the city he is born into is no longer the city his parents married in. The Catholic Monarchs took it by capitulation on the second of January 1492; the last Nasrid sultan has ridden out to the Alpujarras. The house speaks Arabic indoors and Castilian in the street. His father's people are clerics and court accountants, men who keep records for a court that has ceased to exist. They name him al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan al-Fasi al-Gharnati, and the last word of it, the Granadan, is already a memory rather than an address.
suggested_refs: The Capitulations of Granada, 25 November 1491, and their terms for the city's Muslims

stops.name: Granada, the quarter empties
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no source places the family in a named quarter of Granada, and the year of their departure is nowhere recorded
stops.campa: On the hill above the river the old Muslim quarter watches the terms of surrender narrow year by year. The capitulations promised property, law, and the faith; within a decade the promises are read one way in the archbishop's palace and another way in the streets. Families who can afford passage begin to sell. The al-Wazzan household is among them. They cross to Africa while the boy is too small to keep the crossing as a memory. He will grow up hearing about the house, the street, the hill above the river, from people who know they will not see any of it again.
suggested_refs: The Albaicin of Granada in the first decade after the conquest

stops.name: Fez, the exiles take a house
stops.date_confidence: disputed; the flight is dated 1492 on the c. 1485 birth chronology and 'soon after his birth' on the c. 1494 one, and the two cannot both be true
stops.campa: Fez receives them as it has received Andalusi exiles for three hundred years, into a quarter where the masons are Granadan and so is the silk and so is the argument in the street about whose fault it was. An uncle of the boy stands well with the Wattasid sultan and carries letters for him, which is a door. The city is a capital and a university at once: madrasas, tanneries, a river running under the streets, a mosque whose lamps are kept lit by charity. The child who arrives here will spend his life describing places. Fez is the first one he learns street by street, with the whole of a childhood to do it in.
suggested_refs: The Andalusi quarter of Fez and its successive waves of Granadan settlement

stops.name: Fez, the courtyard of al-Qarawiyyin
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the schooling is attested, the year is not, and the range of 1492 to 1507 given in circulating summaries is impossible at both ends
stops.campa: He is set first to the neighbourhood Qur'an school, then to the madrasas, then to al-Qarawiyyin, whose courtyard has been teaching law and grammar and the sciences of the stars since a merchant's daughter endowed it six hundred years before. He learns Maliki jurisprudence and the sciences of the Arabic language, and with them the habit that will make his book: a method that records what a place holds, who governs it, what it grows, what it pays, and what its people say of themselves. The training is meant for a judge or a secretary. It produces a geographer.
suggested_refs: The University of al-Qarawiyyin, founded 859 by Fatima al-Fihri

stops.name: Fez, the notary of the hospital
stops.date_confidence: inferred; attested by a single source, World History Encyclopedia, and undated there
stops.campa: To pay for the years of study he takes work as a notary in one of the city's hospitals, writing out the instruments by which poor men and dying men settle what little they have. It is a long apprenticeship in listening to strangers account for their lives in the exact order the law requires: name, lineage, city, holdings, debts, witnesses. He is a refugee's son with no land of his own, and the work pays him to practise the one form of writing a whole society has agreed to trust. Nothing in his later book will be organized very differently.
suggested_refs: The maristan and charitable foundations of early sixteenth-century Fez

stops.name: Safi, the Portuguese come ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the occupation, which Wikipedia dates to 1508 with Portuguese influence from 1488; his own presence as a boy of about twelve is a dating anchor traceable to Davis and could not be found in the sources cited for it
stops.campa: On the Atlantic coast the Portuguese turn a trading station into a garrison, and Safi is theirs outright. The Moroccan shore is being taken port by port in these years, Ceuta long since, then Agadir, then Azemmour, then this, while the interior stays in the hands of a dynasty that cannot relieve any of them. Scholars date his birth by placing him here, a boy of about twelve, watching it happen. Whether he stood on that beach or not, this is the world his working life will be spent inside: a Maghreb losing its coasts from the sea and holding its deserts from the south.
suggested_refs: The Portuguese occupation of Safi, 1508, and the chain of Atlantic presidios
sources: Natalie Zemon Davis, Trickster Travels (2006), not consulted directly

stops.name: Fez, given a road to travel
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the mission is attested, the year of his first departure from Fez is not
stops.campa: The Wattasid sultan governs a kingdom with an ocean shut against it and a Sahara open behind it, and he keeps men who can ride and write. The uncle who carries his letters takes the nephew along. The office is small and the education is enormous: a young secretary attached to an embassy, expected to draft, to interpret, and to remember what he is shown. He leaves Fez as a functionary of a court losing its coastline, and he will come back with a knowledge of Africa that nobody in Europe possesses and that nobody in Europe will read for another forty years.
suggested_refs: The Wattasid sultanate of Fez and its trans-Saharan diplomacy

stops.name: Sijilmasa, the gate that is not there
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source routes his caravan through Sijilmasa, and his description of it may record a separate journey
stops.campa: The road south begins at the Tafilalt, where for six hundred years the gold of the Sudan came up out of the sand and turned into coin. Sijilmasa was that gate. He finds it destroyed, the walls open, the former residents moved out into the outlying villages and castles, the trade running past the corpse of the town rather than through it. He writes the ruin down without lament, the way a notary writes down a debt: what it was, what became of it, who lives there now. The caravan waters and goes on into country where towns stand three weeks apart.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Sijilmasa near Rissani, abandoned in 1393
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sijilmasa', quoting Leo Africanus on the town's dispersal
Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on Numidia

stops.name: Taghaza, the houses of salt
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia states he visited around 1510 and stayed three days, though how much of his account of the salt trade is eyewitness remains disputed
stops.campa: In the middle of the Sahara there is a place where the ground is salt and nothing else, where the miners cut the floor into slabs and build their houses out of what they dig because there is no other material within reach. The wells are brackish. He stays three days and complains about the water. From here the slabs go south by camel to be traded, weight against weight in the story Europeans will later tell, for the gold of the Niger. He has come out of a university city into the plainest economy on earth: rock that men cannot live without, carried to men who have gold and no rock.
suggested_refs: The Taghaza salt workings in the Taoudenni region, cut and carried south by caravan
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on Numidia

stops.name: Timbuktu, the caravan comes in
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mission, dated c. 1510; the season is not recorded
stops.campa: The embassy from Fez reaches the city on the bend of the Niger and finds it Songhai, taxed and garrisoned from Gao, and rich. The mud walls of Djinguereber have stood three hundred years. He is a young Maghrebi secretary with Maliki law and good Arabic, which in this city is a passport: the scholars here read the books he read in Fez, argue the same commentaries, and correspond with his teachers. He is not an explorer arriving among strangers. He is a lawyer arriving among colleagues at the far end of a very long road.
stops.quote: I my selfe am acquainted with Abu Bacr, sirnamed Pargama, the kings brother, who is blacke in colour, but most beautifull in minde and conditions
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. II, p. 143, of a town of the Niger near Timbuktu
suggested_refs: The Djinguereber Mosque of Timbuktu, built 1327
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the land of the blacks
Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, verified on Internet Archive

stops.name: Timbuktu, the court and the book market
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit; the passage itself was composed in Rome some fifteen years afterward, from memory
stops.campa: He counts what a notary counts. The king keeps judges, doctors and clerics and pays them well. Salt comes in from the desert and is dear. Manuscripts come up from Barbary and are dearer, and the men who deal in them take more profit than any other trade in the city. Fifteen years later, writing in Italian in a rented room in Rome, he will set that sentence down for readers who have never heard of the place, and it will do more than any other line he writes to raise a legend he did not intend: a city of gold at the end of the world.
stops.quote: And hither are brought diuers manuscripts or written bookes out of Barbarie, which are sold for more money than any other merchandize.
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. III, pp. 825-826
suggested_refs: The manuscript libraries of Timbuktu and the Barbary book trade
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. III, verified on Internet Archive

stops.name: Gao, the Askia's capital
stops.date_confidence: disputed; some biographers read the account of Gao as eyewitness and others as an informant's report folded into his own narrative voice
stops.campa: Askia Muhammad rules the Songhai from Gao, having taken the throne by force and legitimacy by pilgrimage, returning from Mecca with a title conferred by the shadow caliph in Cairo. His empire runs from the western bend of the Niger to the edge of the Hausa cities. The description that survives is exact about the court, the currency, the price of a horse and the conduct of the market, exact enough that scholars still argue over whether the man who wrote it stood in that square or listened very carefully to someone who had.
suggested_refs: The Tomb of Askia at Gao, raised by Askia Muhammad I, r. 1493-1528
sources: Natalie Zemon Davis, Trickster Travels (2006), not consulted directly

stops.name: Marrakech, under the Kutubiyya
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; no external source dates or confirms the visit
stops.campa: The southern capital has been fought over by Portuguese, Wattasids, and the rising Saadians out of the Sous, and it shows. He describes ruined palaces, quarters gone back to garden, a population that no longer fills the walls the Almohads raised for it. The Kutubiyya still stands over the emptied ground. He is writing the decline of one Moroccan capital while living in another, and he does not moralize about it; he records how many houses, which trades, which gates, in the manner he was taught to record an estate.
suggested_refs: The Kutubiyya Mosque and the Almohad walls of Marrakech
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Marrakesh

stops.name: Rabat, the kasbah above the Bou Regreg
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; the coordinate is the Kasbah of the Udayas in Rabat, opposite Sale, and no source dates his passage through either town
stops.campa: Two towns face each other across the mouth of a river, Sale on one bank and the Almohad fortress on the other, and between them a bar of sand that decides which ships can come in. This coast is a frontier: Portuguese fleets to the south, Castilian to the north, corsairs already working out of both banks. He surveys it as an official of the court that still holds it, counting harbours his sultan can use. Within a century the two towns will be a republic of pirates, and men taken at sea will be sold on the beach below him.
suggested_refs: The Kasbah of the Udayas at the mouth of the Bou Regreg, opposite Sale
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Fez

stops.name: Taza, the gate in the corridor
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; no external source dates the passage
stops.campa: Between the Rif and the Middle Atlas the land narrows to a single pass, and whoever holds the fortress in it holds the road from Morocco into Algeria. Every dynasty that has ever taken Fez came through here first. He records the place as what it is, a strategic gate with a town attached: walls, garrison, water, and the traffic of a country whose two halves must speak to each other through one corridor. The book he will write reads like a survey of who can reach whom, and by which road, kept by a man whose sultan needs to know.
suggested_refs: The Taza gap between the Rif and the Middle Atlas
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Fez

stops.name: Oujda, the frontier market
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; no external source dates the passage
stops.campa: At the eastern edge of what Fez can call its own, a market town changes hands between the sultans of Morocco and the Zayyanids of Tlemcen whenever either is strong enough to take it. He places it at the border in his account, which is a political statement dressed as geography. The merchants here deal with both kingdoms and pay whichever is nearer. He is travelling east now, beyond his own sultan's writ, into a Maghreb where Spain holds the ports and the Ottomans are beginning to answer.
suggested_refs: Oujda on the Moroccan-Zayyanid frontier
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Fez

stops.name: Tlemcen, the Zayyanid seat
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; no external source dates the passage
stops.campa: The city of the Zayyanids keeps scholars, a mint, a great mosque and the terminus of a caravan road, and keeps them by paying tribute in one direction or another. Spain has taken Oran a day's ride away; the Ottomans are moving on Algiers to the east. He describes a court of learning and trade that everyone around it has already decided is a prize. What he sets down is the central Maghreb in the last years it still belongs to its own dynasties, with the tolls and the prices written in.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Tlemcen and the Zayyanid court
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Tlemcen

stops.name: Oran, the Spanish port
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish seizure of 1509 is attested; his own presence in a Spanish-held port is not established and the visit is reconstruction
stops.campa: Cardinal Cisneros paid for the fleet out of his own revenues and the city fell in a day in 1509. Now the crosses are up over a Muslim port and the garrison lives behind its walls, trading with a country it cannot govern. He records the seizure and the town. Whether he walked in it is another question, since a Wattasid envoy inside a Spanish presidio is a delicate proposition and the record does not say. He is compiling the coastline of a continent being taken from the sea inward, and Oran is the sharpest instance of it he knows.
suggested_refs: The Spanish capture of Oran, 1509, under Cardinal Cisneros
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Tlemcen

stops.name: Bejaia, the harbour under new colours
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish capture of 1510 by Pedro Navarro is attested; his own presence is not established
stops.campa: Pedro Navarro took Bougie from its Hafsid ruler in 1510, and the Spanish hold the harbour while the mountains behind it stay out of their reach. This coast is now a chain: Oran, Bejaia, Tripoli, Spanish; Algiers about to call in the Barbarossa brothers and become something else altogether. He writes the port down among the towns of the Hafsid coast, in the book he gives to Tunis, because that is where it belongs by law even in the years when it does not belong there by garrison.
suggested_refs: The Spanish seizure of Bougie from Sultan Abdelaziz, 1510
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Tunis

stops.name: Tunis, the Hafsid capital
stops.date_confidence: the description is his own; no external source dates this passage, and his later association with the city belongs to a different decade entirely
stops.campa: The Hafsids have ruled here since the Almohad empire broke apart, and their capital is the eastern anchor of everything he has been surveying: the Zaytuna and its scholars, the souks arranged by trade, the road down to the Sahel and the olive country, the harbour at La Goulette. He gives Tunis a whole book of its own. Thirty years later, in the only report anyone will ever make of his old age, a German orientalist will set out for this city to find him, and will not arrive, and after that there is nothing.
suggested_refs: The Zaytuna Mosque and the Hafsid capital of Tunis
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on the kingdom of Tunis

stops.name: Susa, four days waiting out the danger
stops.date_confidence: attested in his own text, which names the town and the delay; the year is not given, and the coordinate is the modern city rather than anything the source supplies
stops.campa: Down the Sahel coast from Tunis, in a walled town of olive merchants, the road ahead is not safe and the traveller stops. Four days. He does not say what the danger was, and no chronicle fills it in for him. The sentence survives because he wrote it in the first person, and because an English translator in 1600 left the first person standing, so that across five hundred years the one thing certainly known about him at this place is that something frightened him for four days and he sat still until it passed.
stops.quote: I my selfe was constrained to stay in this towne for fower daies, in regarde of the danger of the time
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. III, p. 727, in the chapter 'Of the towne of Susa'
suggested_refs: Pory's chapter 'Of the towne of Susa', preceding 'Of the towne of Monaster'
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. III, verified on Internet Archive

segments.name: East, in the Year of Selim

stops.name: Constantinople, an embassy to the sultan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mission and the year; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: Sultan Muhammad al-Burtughali of Fez sends him east to the one Muslim power still expanding. Selim I has taken Syria and is finishing Egypt; within a year the Ottoman sultan will hold the keys of Mecca and call himself servant of the two sanctuaries. The envoy of a kingdom losing its ports to Portugal arrives in the capital of an empire swallowing a continent. He is perhaps in his early thirties, he has crossed the Sahara and the whole Maghreb, and he stands now in the one city that can see both ends of the Mediterranean at once.
suggested_refs: The court of Selim I at Constantinople in the year of the Egyptian conquest

stops.name: Alexandria, the delta gate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Egyptian itinerary in the sources names Rosetta, Cairo and Aswan and does not name Alexandria, and his own Rosetta passage places Selim there rather than himself
stops.campa: The old Greek city is a shrunken port with its lighthouse gone and its harbour still working, the door through which Egypt has always been entered from the sea. Selim passes through it in the year of the conquest. Whether the traveller did is recorded nowhere that survives; the accounts that put him here are completing a route rather than reporting a stop. What is certain is that in this year he is somewhere in the delta, moving between the Mediterranean and Cairo while an empire changes hands around him.
suggested_refs: Alexandria under the first year of Ottoman rule
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on Egypt
Wikipedia, 'Leo Africanus', which omits Alexandria from the itinerary

stops.name: Rasid, the sultan passes through
stops.date_confidence: attested; he places himself in the town and dates himself by Selim's passage, though he gives no day
stops.campa: At Rosetta on the western branch of the Nile, a town of fishermen and customs officers, the conqueror of Egypt comes back down the road from Alexandria with his intimates and stops to look at a bath house. The Mamluk sultanate has been dead a few months. The man watching is a Moroccan envoy with no business in this war whatever. The battle and the executions go unrecorded by him. What he keeps is a sovereign taking pleasure in a building. He writes it down, and it is one of the few times he tells us exactly where he stood.
stops.quote: I my selfe was in this citie when Selim the great Turke returned this way from Alexandria, who with his priuate and familiar friends beholding the said bath-stoue, seemed to take great delight and contentment therein.
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. III, p. 866
suggested_refs: The bath house at Rasid noted in Pory's marginal gloss, 'John Leo was at Rasid the same time when Turke passed this way'
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. III, verified on Internet Archive

stops.name: Cairo, al-Azhar in the year of the conquest
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: Cairo has just stopped being the capital of an empire and started being the second city of another. Tuman Bay was hanged at the Zuwayla gate in April; the last caliph of the Abbasid shadow line is being taken north to Istanbul. Al-Azhar goes on teaching. He walks a city of half a million people, larger than anything he has seen and larger than anything in Europe, and he sets down its quarters, its trades, its river and its ruins with the same instrument he used on a salt mine in the Sahara. Egypt gets a book of its own.
suggested_refs: The al-Azhar Mosque and university of Cairo in 1517
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on Egypt

stops.name: Aswan, the edge of the survey
stops.date_confidence: attested for the journey up the Nile; the season is not recorded
stops.campa: He goes south up the river as far as the first cataract, where Egypt ends and boats must be dragged over rock, and the country beyond belongs to Nubians and to the Funj and to no sultan he serves. This is the far corner of the world he will describe, matched at the other end by the Atlantic surf at Safi and at the bottom by the Niger. From here the route bends east toward the Red Sea ports, and from here the record of his movements grows thinner at every stage until it is only supposition.
suggested_refs: The First Cataract at Aswan, southern limit of Ottoman Egypt
sources: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa, book on Egypt

stops.name: Mecca, the pilgrim's supposition
stops.date_confidence: disputed; the hajj is inferred from his route and his standing, is not narrated in his surviving text, and French sources place the later capture on a voyage returning from Mecca while others have him sailing from Cairo
stops.campa: A Muslim of learning, in Arabia, in the season, with the crossing already made: the inference is easy and the evidence is nothing. His own book, which gives the price of a horse in Gao and the state of the water at Taghaza, does not describe the rite. He is thirty or thereabouts, and he has by now travelled more of the Islamic world than almost anyone living. If he circled the House, he never wrote it down, or he wrote it in a manuscript that did not survive, or he wrote it in Rome and thought better of the sentence.
suggested_refs: The hajj season of 1518, the first under Ottoman guardianship of the holy cities

stops.name: Gerbi, taken by the corsairs
stops.date_confidence: attested for the capture in 1518; the place is contradicted, Pory naming the isle of Gerbi while Wikipedia weights Crete as more probable, and the corsairs are called Italian, Spanish and probably Venetian in three different accounts
stops.campa: Somewhere on the summer sea between Egypt and home, a Christian galley takes the ship he is travelling in. His own translator prints the fact as a chapter heading over the island of Djerba; other accounts put it off Crete; the pirates are Italian in one telling, Spanish in another, probably Venetian in a third. Nobody agrees where or by whom. What everyone agrees is that a diplomat carrying letters became, in an afternoon, a piece of cargo, and that the cargo was judged too valuable to sell in the ordinary market.
stops.quote: Of the isle of Gerbi or Zerbi, where Iohn Leo the Author of this Historie was taken by Italian pirates, and carried thence to Rome
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. III, pp. 733-734, chapter title within the book on Tunis
suggested_refs: Pory's chapter heading on Gerbi, the earliest printed statement of the capture
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. III, verified on Internet Archive
Robert Brown, Introduction, Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. I, p. xli

stops.name: Rhodes, in the hands of the Knights
stops.date_confidence: attested for the imprisonment; the length of the detention is not recorded
stops.campa: The Knights Hospitaller have held this island for two centuries and live off the sea war, and their prisons are full of Muslims taken in it. He is put among them. Someone examines him for ransom value and finds a man carrying Maliki law, four languages, an embassy's credentials and a memory of Timbuktu. Captives like that do not go to the galleys. They go to Rome as a gift. Four years from now Suleiman will take this island and turn the Knights out; the man they sent away will be a Christian by then.
suggested_refs: The Palace of the Grand Master at Rhodes, held by the Hospitallers until 1522

stops.name: Rome, the cell in Castel Sant'Angelo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the detention; its length and exact dates are not recorded, and no source documents the route by which he was carried through Italy
stops.campa: Hadrian's tomb has been a fortress and a papal prison for a thousand years, and he is held inside it. Leo X is a Medici who buys manuscripts, keeps orientalists, blesses Portuguese ventures down the African coast and wants Arabic taught in Rome. What has been delivered to him is a living index of a continent no European has crossed. The questioning that follows is the beginning of the book: a captive answering questions about Fez and the Niger for men who have only Ptolemy and rumour, and who do not stop asking.
suggested_refs: Castel Sant'Angelo, papal fortress and prison

segments.name: Rome, and the Name of Leo

stops.name: Rome, baptized in Saint Peter's
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year by Wikipedia and for the day, the Feast of the Epiphany, by World History Encyclopedia; the claim that freedom was conditioned on baptism is in no reachable source and is not carried here
stops.campa: On the Feast of the Epiphany, in the old basilica that Bramante is dismantling around the ceremony, al-Hasan al-Wazzan is baptized and given the pope's own two names: Giovanni Leone de' Medici. Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo stands as godfather. Whether liberty was the price or the consequence, no document says, and the bargain that everyone repeats is in none of them. He walks from the font with a Medici name, a pension, and a language he cannot yet write. Europe will call him by neither name he was given, but Leo the African.
stops.quote: E indusse a farsi Christiano & gli pose in due suoi nomi, Giodansi & Leone
stops.quote_source: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Delle navigationi et viaggi, quoted in Robert Brown's Introduction to The History and Description of Africa, Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. I, p. xlii, n. 2
suggested_refs: The old Constantinian basilica of Saint Peter, then half demolished for Bramante's rebuilding

stops.name: Rome, teaching Arabic in the papal circle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the teaching and the patronage; the range is bounded by Leo X's death on 1 December 1521, and his work on Egidio's Latin Qur'an is separately dated 1525
stops.campa: In the household of Egidio da Viterbo, general of the Augustinians and a serious Arabist, the convert becomes a teacher. He gives Arabic to churchmen, corrects a Latin Qur'an, compiles a grammar and a vocabulary of medical terms, writes lives of illustrious Arabs for readers who know none of them. He is learning Italian at the same rate his students are learning his tongue. The man who spent his youth being paid to record other men's estates is now being paid to record his entire world, from memory, for people who have no way to check him.
suggested_refs: Egidio da Viterbo's Arabic and Hebrew scholarly household in Rome

stops.name: Rome, the pope dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for Leo X's death on 1 December 1521; his own departure follows under Adrian VI, elected January 1522 and resident in Rome from August 1522, and the suspicion motive is interpretive rather than sourced
stops.campa: Leo X dies at forty-five with the treasury empty, Luther excommunicated, and the Medici position in Italy unresolved. The Roman circle scatters. The pope elected after him is a Dutch ascetic who buys no manuscripts, keeps no orientalists and has no use for a court of humanists, and Rome detests him for it. The African, whose entire standing in the city rested on one man's curiosity, has nothing left to stand on. He leaves, and spends three or four years moving about in the north, and the record of him goes intermittent for the first time since Rhodes.
suggested_refs: The conclave of 1521-1522 and the election of Adrian VI

stops.name: Bologna, the grammar in the university town
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Bologna years, roughly 1522 to 1525; the arrival itself is not dated
stops.campa: In a university city with a Hebrew press and a settled community of Jewish scholars, he works on Arabic language material and on a vocabulary of medical terms, some of it in collaboration. Only fragments survive. He is one of perhaps a dozen men in Europe who can do this work at all, and he is doing it for a continent that has not decided whether he is a scholar, a trophy, a convert of convenience, or a leftover from a dead pope's household. What he is not doing, in any way the record shows, is trying to get home.
suggested_refs: The surviving Bologna fragments of an Arabic grammar and a medical vocabulary

stops.name: Rome, under the second Medici pope
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia dates the return to Rome to 1526 under Clement VII, so the Roman residence under Clement runs 1526 to 1527 and not the longer range sometimes printed
stops.campa: Clement VII is a Medici again, and the African is called back to the city that first held him prisoner. He has been in Italy eight years. He has Italian now, and Latin, and a hand that can draft; he has outlived the patron who made him and one pope in between. The commission, whether it was ever formally given or simply understood, is the one thing he alone can supply: everything he saw between the Atlantic and the Nile, and everything he heard from men who saw the rest, set down in order, in a language Europe can read.
suggested_refs: The papal court of Clement VII in the year before the sack

stops.name: Rome, the manuscript finished
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1526 by Wikipedia, while World History Encyclopedia gives 1527; the month is not recorded in either
stops.campa: He finishes it in Italian, a language he learned at thirty, and calls it a cosmography and geography of Africa: seven books, the kingdoms of Marrakesh, Fez, Tlemcen and Tunis, then Numidia, then the land of the blacks, then Egypt. It is the first account of the interior of the continent by a man who crossed it, addressed to readers who had Ptolemy and sailors' tales and nothing in between. Somewhere in it he sets down the sentence about his two countries, and it is the only line in the whole survey where he says what the arrangement costs.
stops.quote: For mine owne part, when I heare the Africans euill spoken of, I wil affirme my selfe to be one of Granada: and when I perceiue the nation of Granada to be discommended, then will I professe my selfe to be an African.
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. I, p. 190; also quoted in Robert Brown's Introduction, p. v, in a slightly different rendering
suggested_refs: The 1526 autograph manuscript, Cosmographia et geographia de Affrica, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Rome, MS V.E. 953
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. I, verified on Internet Archive

stops.name: Rome, the sack
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sack, which begins 6 May 1527; his own movements at and after it are nowhere recorded
stops.campa: The unpaid imperial army comes over the walls on the sixth of May, kills for a week, and holds the city for months afterward. The pope is besieged in Castel Sant'Angelo, where the African was once a prisoner. The Roman humanist world ends in that summer: presses broken, libraries burned, scholars dead or dispersed to Venice and Bologna and France. From this point there is no further trace of Giovanni Leone de' Medici in any Italian archive. He is somewhere between thirty-three and forty-two years old, and the record simply stops.
suggested_refs: The Sack of Rome, 6 May 1527, and the dispersal of the papal humanist circle
sources: Natalie Zemon Davis, Trickster Travels (2006), not consulted directly

stops.name: Tunis, the report of a return
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the return to North Africa is undated and the reversion to Islam rests on Widmannstetter's sixteenth-century report rather than on any act, deed or witness
stops.campa: The one thread that survives is a German's abandoned plan. Johann Albrecht Widmannstetter, orientalist and Hebraist, intends to travel to Tunis to meet the man who has by then returned to Islam, and never makes the journey. That is the whole of it: a scholar's cancelled itinerary, naming a city and stating a fact. No abjuration, no deed, no letter, no witness who arrived. He is al-Hasan al-Wazzan again in the report of a man who never saw him, and there is nothing else on the far side of Rome.
suggested_refs: Johann Albrecht Widmannstetter's planned and abandoned journey to Tunis

stops.name: Tunis, the emperor takes the city
stops.date_confidence: attested for the conquest of Tunis by Charles V in July 1535; whether he was in the city, or alive at all, is entirely conjectural
stops.campa: Charles V lands with a fleet, takes Tunis from Barbarossa, restores a Hafsid client and turns the army loose on the town. The sea he was captured on has become the front line between two empires. One reconstruction of his last years has him living here when it happens and leaving for Morocco rather than staying under a Christian garrison, which would make it the second time in one life that he moved because a Christian sovereign took the city he lived in. There is no evidence for it beyond the shape of the story.
suggested_refs: The conquest of Tunis by Charles V, July 1535
sources: Wikipedia, 'Leo Africanus', third theory of his later life

stops.name: Fez, a supposed last return
stops.date_confidence: conjecture; no document places him in Fez after 1518, and this date is a placeholder inside a reconstruction that carries no dates of its own
stops.campa: In the version that has him leaving Tunis, he ends where he was raised, in the city of exiles that took his family in when Granada closed. Fez by now is falling to the Saadians out of the south, and the Wattasid dynasty he served is in its last decade. No document places him there. It is the ending the story wants, the man of two countries returning to the one that fed and taught him, and the honest description of it is that nobody knows and everybody has a preference.
suggested_refs: The Saadian conquest of Fez and the end of the Wattasid sultanate
sources: Wikipedia, 'Leo Africanus', third theory of his later life

stops.name: Tunis, a death without a grave
stops.date_confidence: conjecture; c. 1554 in Tunis is the conventional date from later Arabic biobibliography, against a rival c. 1550 in Rome, and French Wikipedia states plainly that no reliable information exists on either the date or the place
stops.campa: The date usually given is around 1554 and the place is usually Tunis, and neither comes from a document. A rival account has him never leaving Christendom at all and dying in Rome about 1550. There is no tomb anywhere, no register, no notice, no line in any chronicle. A man who wrote down the population of towns three weeks apart in the Sahara, who recorded the weight of a king's gold and the price of a manuscript, left no record whatsoever of his own end, in either of his religions.
suggested_refs: The absence of any documented tomb or burial place, stated as such in French Wikipedia

stops.name: Venice, Ramusio puts it in print
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1550 printing in the first volume of Delle navigationi et viaggi
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after the sack, a Venetian civil servant with a passion for travel accounts prints the manuscript in the first volume of his Navigationi et viaggi, and the book enters Europe without its author. It is reprinted and reprinted. What Europe takes from it is not the notary's ledger of towns and taxes but one glittering paragraph: a king with plates and scepters of gold, and salt worth more than either. Timbuktu becomes a rumour of treasure, and men will die in the desert for three centuries looking for the city in that sentence.
stops.quote: The rich king of Tombuto hath many plates and scepters of gold, some whereof weigh 1300. poundes: and he keepes a magnificent and well furnished court.
stops.quote_source: Leo Africanus, The History and Description of Africa, trans. John Pory (1600), Hakluyt Society ed. 1896, vol. III, p. 824
suggested_refs: Giovanni Battista Ramusio, Delle navigationi et viaggi, vol. I, Venice 1550
sources: Pory trans., Hakluyt Soc. 1896, vol. III, verified on Internet Archive

stops.name: London, Pory's English
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1600 publication; the translation was made from the Latin version rather than from the Italian original, and carries its errors
stops.campa: John Pory englishes it as A Geographical Historie of Africa, working from the Latin rather than the Italian, which imports errors that will be copied for three hundred years. He also keeps something better than accuracy: the first person. Every place in the book where the author says I my selfe was in this citie, or I my selfe was constrained to stay, comes through into English intact. So the only voice that survives of a man with no grave and no death date speaks Elizabethan, and stays the standard English reference on the continent until Europeans begin going to look.
suggested_refs: John Pory, A Geographical Historie of Africa, London 1600; Hakluyt Society reprint, 3 vols., 1896

stops.name: London, the Moor on the stage
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the suggestion that Shakespeare used Pory while preparing Othello is a scholarly proposal and is not documented
stops.campa: Three years after Pory, a play is written about a Moor in Venetian service who tells his history in a room and is destroyed by a European who understands his position better than he does. Scholars have long proposed that the playwright had the new translation on his desk. It cannot be shown. What can be shown is that within a single generation the only book by an African that Europe possessed had become raw material for a European story about Africans, which is what happens to the book from then on.
suggested_refs: The proposed use of Pory's translation in the composition of Othello, c. 1603

stops.name: Paris, the life given back as a novel
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication of Amin Maalouf's Leon l'Africain in 1986
stops.campa: A Lebanese writer in France, himself a man of two countries, writes the missing autobiography: four hundred pages in the first person, Granada to Fez to Timbuktu to Rome, filling every silence the documents left with invention and saying openly that it is invention. It becomes the way most readers meet him. Twenty years later a historian assembles the documented version and argues for the return to Islam. Between the novel that admits it is inventing and the archive that admits it cannot reach him, the man stays where he has been since 1527, out of sight.
suggested_refs: Amin Maalouf, Leon l'Africain (Paris, 1986); Natalie Zemon Davis, Trickster Travels (New York, 2006)
sources: Natalie Zemon Davis, Trickster Travels (Hill & Wang, 2006), not consulted directly
